comment: The wire-format fixtures both readers of a runbook release share.
scripts/check-release reads these in Python and crates/htmlspec-cli/src/runbook_release.rs
reads them in Rust, because the release check runs where no build has happened. Sharing the
fixtures rather than the code is what keeps the two from disagreeing about version ordering
or about what a legacy archive is: a rule stated twice is a rule that diverges, and the
divergence surfaces as a suite that passes locally and fails in continuous integration.
Each case carries the reason it exists, because a fixture whose purpose is unstated is one
a later contributor deletes to make a failure go away.

inventories.why: The ordinary shape: two runbooks, each with both fingerprints and its changelog snapshot.
An empty inventory is a record, not an absence: a missing file and a file saying 'there were no runbooks' are different facts, and only the second is a record.
Two entries for one runbook leave the predecessor question unanswerable.
A digest in another form would compare unequal to the same content, which reads as a changed document.
An unknown field is a fact neither reader would read, so it is refused rather than ignored.
A format this program does not read is not a history it can order.
The changelog is carried as a snapshot so a deleted or renamed runbook cannot make a past release unverifiable.
An inventory of none states an empty list rather than omitting it, so the two cannot be confused.

adoptions.why: The ordinary shape: the first project version subject to inventories.
A marker in a format this program does not read cannot say when the obligation began.
A marker names the version adopted at; without one there is no beginning to the history.
The marker is never advanced on a later release, so a field claiming an advance is refused rather than read.

comparisons.name: the-first-release
comparisons.why: A runbook with no prior snapshot publishes at any version above 0.0.0.

comparisons.name: the-first-release-at-the-unreleased-version
comparisons.why: 0.0.0 is the version a runbook carries before it has been released at all.

comparisons.name: unchanged-content-at-one-version
comparisons.why: Identical content at the same version is one release snapshotted twice, not a duplicate release.

comparisons.name: a-version-only-release

current.name: release
current.changelog:
# Changelog

## 0.2.0

A second release.

## 0.1.0

The first.

comparisons.why: An unchanged runbook may advance its version with a matching changelog entry.

comparisons.name: changed-content-without-a-bump
comparisons.why: One version must not identify two different released contracts.

comparisons.name: changed-procedure-without-a-bump
comparisons.why: A changed procedure is a changed release whichever document moved.

comparisons.name: a-downgrade-with-identical-content

release.name: release
release.changelog:
# Changelog

## 0.2.0

A second release.

## 0.1.0

The first.

current.name: release
current.changelog:
# Changelog

## 0.2.0

A second release.

## 0.1.0

The first.

comparisons.why: The gate is an ordering rather than a difference test, and this is the case that separates them: the content did not differ.

comparisons.name: a-release-its-changelog-does-not-head
comparisons.why: A carried runbook identifies its release by the version and the heading together.

comparisons.name: a-release-its-changelog-heads-twice
comparisons.why: A changelog heading one version twice cannot say which entry is the release.

comparisons.name: a-renamed-runbook-begins-a-new-lineage
comparisons.why: Identity is the directory name, so a rename starts a new lineage above 0.0.0 rather than continuing the old one.

comparisons.name: a-second-runbook-at-the-same-version
comparisons.why: Distinctness is per runbook, so two runbooks may each be at 0.1.0.
